title: Interaction renormalization and the plasma staircase
authors: Alexander V. Milovanov, Alexander Iomin, Jens Juul Rasmussen
abstract: We resolve an existing question concerning dynamical and structural stability of the E {\times} B staircases in magnetically confined fusion plasma. The problem has stirred considerable interest in the literature due to a unique combination of its scientific and practical aspects. Here, we report a new approach to the problem by combining the paradigmatic Hasegawa-Wakatani model of electrostatic drift-wave turbulence with an idea of interaction renormalization, imported from quantum field theory. It is shown based on the Schrödinger-Newton equation with renormalized interaction constant that the plasma staircase is robust and stable as soon as the nonadiabaticity parameter, δ, goes above a certain critical value, and is unstable otherwise. This critical value is an exact result of the interaction model and is found to be δc = π. For δ < δc , the unstable system expands in the radial direction, resulting in a radial second moment that grows with time t as t^(2/3). The results obtained bear important implications with regard to the implementation of arrays of semipermeable transport barriers in tokamaks, suggesting a threshold condition for their generation.
summary: This theoretical work investigates the stability of plasma structures called E x B staircases in fusion reactors by merging the Hasegawa-Wakatani model with quantum field theory concepts like interaction renormalization. The study establishes a precise critical threshold ($\delta_c = \pi$) determining whether these barriers are stable or prone to radial expansion, suggesting a fundamental physical condition for plasma confinement.
main_problem: The paper addresses the dynamical and structural stability of E x B staircases in magnetically confined fusion plasma.
main_result: The plasma staircase is stable only when the nonadiabaticity parameter exceeds a critical value, $\delta_c = \pi$. Below this threshold, the system exhibits instability characterized by a specific growth rate of its radial second moment.
method: The authors combine the Hasegawa-Wakatani model with interaction renormalization techniques borrowed from quantum field theory, leading to a mean-field description via the Schrödinger-Newton equation.
model_or_system: The system models plasma dynamics in a tokamak, governed by a Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation (NLSE) derived from the HW model. The nonlinearity is modified by an interaction renormalization constant, leading to a subquadratic nonlinearity.
key_observables: The stability of the plasma staircase, the radial second moment growth rate ($\propto t^{2/3}$ for instability), and the critical nonadiabaticity parameter $\delta_c$.
important_parameters: The nonadiabaticity parameter ($\delta$), the critical value ($\delta_c = \pi$), and the nonlinearity exponent ($s$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mean-field approximations, the use of the HW model, and the incorporation of interaction renormalization from QFT.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the NLSE model, showing elliptic contours representing staircase jets, dashed arrows indicating avalanches/voids, and the direction of E x B drift.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical problem (plasma stability) to introducing the theoretical framework (HW model + interaction renormalization) and culminates in deriving the stability criteria and the critical threshold $\delta_c$.
why_interesting: The application of concepts like interaction renormalization and subquadratic nonlinearity, typically seen in quantum field theory or disordered systems, to a classical plasma problem provides a rich analogy for understanding non-equilibrium critical phenomena.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: The NLSE model. Elliptic contours (gray color) rep- resent staircase jets circling around the magnetic flux surfaces. Each such contour is thought of as a nonlinear oscillator char- acterized by the radial position xj, wave number nj = 2π/lj, and rotation period Tj = lj/u, where u is the E × B velocity. Dashed arrows represent respectively avalanches (red color) and voids (green color). Gray arrows indicate the direction of the E × B drift. The tokamak core is depicted as a central oval (violet color).
